conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays confidential within your medical team, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go one question at a own pace, and if anything feels overwhelming we can pause. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things as much as you usually do?

[soft half-smile, eyes a little tired]  
Um… I guess not quite as much. I still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes that silly face at the baby—but it feels muted, like I have to remind myself to enjoy it. Most of the time I’m just… tired, so even funny things don’t hit the same way they used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… that’s pretty much what I meant. I can still laugh, just not as easily or as often as before she was born.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow shrug, eyes drop to the blanket]  
Not really. I mean, I’ll still think “It’ll be nice to get coffee with my friend next week,” but the second that thought’s gone, I’m back to feeling… flat. Even little outings feel like chores I have to force myself to get ready for.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes. If she won’t settle at night, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m not doing something right—like I’m missing some trick the other moms know. Or when I have to give her a bottle instead of nursing longer, I feel guilty, even though she’s gaining fine. It’s not constant, just these little jabs a few times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… a lot of the time it’s about her breathing. I’ll stare at the baby monitor even when she’s asleep, sure something’s wrong even though she looks fine. Or I’ll worry that the formula isn’t the right kind, or that the room’s too cold, too warm—just random things that I know are probably okay but my mind keeps circling back to.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrapping the blanket tighter around my shoulders]  
A couple of times. Like last night, I was feeding her in the dark and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get a full breath. It lasted maybe five minutes. Nothing was wrong, but I kept thinking, “What if something happens and I can’t help her?” It passed, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep when she sleeps, it feels like the next thing’s already piling up before I finish the last. I’ll finally sit down and remember I haven’t eaten or showered, and suddenly I’m on the verge of tears—not sobbing, just this tight, heavy feeling that I can’t quite keep up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not so much “unhappy” as… keyed-up. Once she’s down for the night my mind keeps replaying every little thing—did I wash the bottles right, is her rash getting worse, will she wake up in an hour? I’ll lie there exhausted but can’t drift off, and when I do, I’m awake again at the tiniest sound. It’s only a few nights a week, but it’s starting to wear on me.
I have felt sad or miserable

Sometimes. It’s not all day, but little waves hit—like when I’m rocking her and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. I’ll think, “I should be happier right now,” and that just makes the sadness feel heavier. It passes, maybe in minutes, maybe an hour, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quietly]  
Only once or twice this week. The other night I finally got her to sleep, and instead of feeling relieved I just sat on the couch and teared up. It wasn’t loud crying—more like quiet tears rolling while I stared at the wall. I couldn’t even explain why.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No. Never. I couldn’t—I want to be here for her. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’d never think of hurting myself.

You've shared that motherhood has felt heavy lately: laughing and looking forward to things are harder, waves of sadness arrive without warning, and worries about your baby race through your mind even when she's safe. You're doing your best-forcing yourself through chores, soothing her at 3 a.m.-yet you often feel flat, tearful, and overwhelmed, with a tight heaviness you can't quite shake.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes near-total loss of anticipatory pleasure, calling even small outings "chores" and feeling "flat," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "sometimes" and "a few times a day," matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive worries about the baby's safety and environment occurring "a lot of the time," matching "Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden racing heart, breathlessness, and fear without cause, occurring "a couple of times"—clearly maps to "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, constant task pile-up, and near-tears when realizing unmet basic needs, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty "only a few nights a week" due to intrusive worries, aligning with "Yes, sometimes" despite avoiding the word "unhappy."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent waves of sadness that keep returning, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 19 places you well above the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>depressive disorder</med> with <med>peripartum onset</med>. Key indicators include <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym> (<quote>little outings feel like chores</quote>), <sym>persistent sadness</sym> (<quote>little waves hit</quote>), <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym> related to depressive rumination, <sym>nearly daily panic</sym>, and <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>. No suicidal ideation endorsed on Q10. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent mental-health appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist within the next week
2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy; ask your clinic for perinatal-specialized therapists
3. Plan daily 15-minute rest periods-accept help from partner, family, or postpartum doula so you can nap or shower
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic</sym> symptoms start; keep lights dim during night feeds to lower arousal
5. Limit monitor-checking to once per hour after bedtime; place baby on back in clear crib to reduce safety worries
6. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks or sooner if mood, anxiety, or sleep worsen; if any thoughts of self-harm emerge seek emergency care immediately
7. Attend local new-mom support group; peer contact lowers <sym>isolation</sym> and normalizes emotional changes
8. Share these results with your pediatrician and OB so the whole care team can coordinate support for you and your baby
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≈ weeks–months old)  
Instrument: EPDS-10 dialogue  
Clinician: ———, LCSW  

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia / reduced pleasure (Q2)  
- Frequent tearfulness, “waves” of sadness (Q8, Q9)  
- Initial insomnia & maintenance insomnia related to racing thoughts (Q7)  
- Daily guilt/self-blame re parenting choices (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety (Q4) and two discrete panic episodes (Q5)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, difficulty coping (Q6)  

Pattern  
Persistent low mood with anxious rumination, no current suicidal ideation (Q10 denied). Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with sleep and self-care.  

Screening significance  
Score pattern consistent with at least moderate postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; rule-out perinatal mood & anxiety disorder.  

Risk factors noted  
- Sleep deprivation secondary to mood  
- Recurrent guilt cognitions  
- Panic symptoms  
- No social withdrawal reported, but diminished anticipatory enjoyment of outings.  

Safety  
Denies self-harm or thoughts of harming infant. No protective concerns voiced.  

Next steps for primary team  
- Provide EPDS-10 numerical score; consider formal assessment with psychiatrist or PMH specialist.  
- Offer psycho-education, support group, CBT/interpersonal therapy referral.  
- Counsel on sleep hygiene, respite options.  
- Re-evaluate mood, anxiety, and safety status within 1–2 weeks or sooner if worsening.
